content:
Yesterday we studied the wilderness camp of Israel and the Levites being cleansed. The water was sprinkled, the razor was applied, the garments were washed; and nothing was left unclean. That picture was not given to us simply as history. Yahweh built it as a shadow of something that would come.

Today we look at ourselves. We are not Levites. But we are separated for his service just like the Levites were separated. Christ said plainly: "You are not of the world; I have chosen you out of the world" (John 15:19). That is the same language. Set apart. Called out. Separated for holy service. And just like the Levites, we too must be cleansed before we can serve. The same three acts apply to us; but now they are deeper, more personal, and more powerful than anything that happened in that wilderness camp.

The Levites received purification water from outside themselves. They could not sprinkle their own heads. Someone else had to do it. This is exactly how our cleansing begins. The Word of God comes to us; through Scripture, through the teaching of Christ and it washes us in a way we could never wash ourselves. Paul writes that Christ cleanses His called-out ones "with the washing of water by the word" (Ephesians 5:26). Christ told his disciples: "Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you" (John 15:3). And in his prayer to the Father he asked: "Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth" (John 17:17). This is where everything begins. The moment we hear the Word, receive it, and believe it; the sprinkling has happened. We are declared clean. We are separated from the world. We are made ready to draw near.

But the cleansing does not end there. The water opens the door. What comes next is harder.

When the Levite had been sprinkled with water, the razor came next. And here is something we must not pass over lightly; the Levite's hair was not trimmed. It was not shaped or shortened. It was completely removed. Hair grows naturally from the flesh. It has been growing since birth. It belongs to the natural, fleshly state of man. Yahweh was not asking for an improvement.

He was asking for complete removal. In the same way, when the Word of God enters our lives and begins to do its deeper work, it does not come to improve the old nature. It comes to cut it away entirely. This is exactly what the writer of Hebrews says: "The word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword" (Hebrews 4:12). That sharpness is not decorative.
It is purposeful. The razor-sharp Word cuts into the places where pride has taken root. It cuts away self-will; the determination to live on our own terms.

It exposes fleshly desires and old habits that we carried with us when we first answered the call. Paul names this work very plainly: "Put off concerning the former conversation the old man" (Ephesians 4:22). And again: "Our old man is crucified with him" (Romans 6:6). Yahweh is not in the business of making the old man more presentable. The old man must go. This means that when the Word convicts us; when it points to something in us that does not belong in a consecrated life, the right response is not to argue or bargain with it. We let it cut. We hold still under the razor. That is how the New Creation is shaped.

After the Levite had been sprinkled and shaved, his garments were washed. The order is important. The inward cleansing came first. The outward followed. Garments in Scripture speak of conduct; the visible, daily life that others see. Ecclesiastes puts it simply: "Let thy garments be always white" (Ecclesiastes 9:8). A man's garments tell you something about where he has been and how he lives. For the New Creation, the washed garments represent a walk before Yahweh and before men that reflects what the water and the razor have already done inside. If the Word has truly washed us and the razor has truly done its cutting work, it will show. It cannot stay hidden. John writes: "If we walk in the light, as he is in the light, the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin" (1 John 1:7). Notice; the cleansing and the walking go together. Isaiah calls out: "Wash you, make you clean" (Isaiah 1:16). Paul puts it even more directly: "Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 13:14). Our garments as New Creation believers are the character of Messiah worn in daily life, in how we speak, how we treat the brethren, how we respond under pressure, how we handle what the world offers us. The clean garments are not a performance. They are the natural outward evidence of a person who has genuinely been through the water and under the razor.

So the three acts flow together as one complete, unbroken work. The Word comes and washes; and we receive it. That same Word, sharp and powerful, begins to cut away the old nature, and we yield to it. And as the old is removed, the new begins to show in the way we live; and the garments become clean. This is Yahweh's way of consecrating the New Creation. Not a ceremony performed once in the wilderness, but a daily, ongoing, deepening work; the same three acts, moving through our lives, until the day we are presented before Him completely set apart and ready.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our Father,

We thank You that You did not leave us to cleanse ourselves.

You sent Your Word; and it found us, washed us, and called us out.

Now we ask for the courage to hold still under the razor.

Let the Word do what trimming cannot do, let it remove the old nature completely.

Where pride still grows, cut it away.

Where self-will still holds on, break it loose.

And let what shows on the outside; in how we walk, speak, and love be the clean garments of a people who have truly been through Your cleansing.

Make us ready for the service You have set before us.

Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits

who forgiveth all thine iniquities, who healeth all thy diseases,

who redeemeth thy life from destruction." Psalm 103:2-4

In Christ name Amen.
